area: Residential feel across Charlottetown: yard profiles per neighbourhood, new neighbourhood entries, mail, carts, school yards, church lawns, playgrounds
yard_profile_schema: generator: the keys scripts/world/town_dressing.gd already reads from map_config.json 'yards' (front/back weights, back_height, shed, trampoline, fire_pit, picnic_table, carts, mailbox_post) - pasteable; extra: shares for features the generator doesn't place yet (wall mailbox, steps/porch kinds, deck, flower beds, hoop, chairs, flags); colours in 'yard_colours'.

North Sherwood._comment: Locals: 'up in Sherwood, off Ash Drive' (Fulton, Conamore, Abbey, Lilac, Ash, Birch Hill, Montgomery, Ferngarden; former Town of Sherwood, east of Mount Edward Road, south of the bypass). OSM: 270 houses, big footprints (median 182 m2), many detached and attached garages, LiDAR median top 6 m (mostly bungalows and split-entries, about a quarter two-storey). Era guess 1980s-2000s. Ash Drive photo (CBC 2023): white bungalow, open lawn, grass boulevard and sidewalk. Colours a guess from era.

Robin Hood Park._comment: North Sherwood past the bypass: Scarlet, Robin and Friar (the Robin Hood names round Robin Hood Park), Norwood Road's west end, Richard Drive, Doncaster. Small low houses (median 135 m2, LiDAR top 4.9 m): 1970s-2000 bungalows (25 Friar Dr built 2000) and, on Friar Drive/Norwood Road, a 66-lot mini-home neighbourhood rezoned in 2021 ('Norwood Estates', 63 Friar a year old) and a 44-unit seniors' building on Norwood Road (CBC). Palette a guess.

Sherwood flower streets._comment: Shamrock Drive, Heather Avenue, east Lilac Avenue, Dale Drive by Brackley Point Road: 1970s low-slope bungalows and split-levels (LiDAR: 53% low or flat roofs, 30% two-storey parts, median 174 m2). Era and palette a guess.

Brighton waterfront._comment: Locals call it Brighton ('Executive Brighton Waterfront' in a Queen Elizabeth Drive listing; 'mature trees line newer developments along Queen Elizabeth, Edinburgh, Inkerman and Prince Charles drives'): the royal-named streets north of Victoria Park by the North River, plus Viceroy, Lansdowne, Harbour Lane, Jubilee. Large one-and-a-half and two-storey houses of the 1950s-70s and later infill on big treed lots (median footprint 200 m2), some brick and stone fronts. West Kent Elementary on Viceroy Avenue. Palette a guess between Brighton's old houses and the suburbs.

Colonel Gray Drive._comment: Between North River Road and the river north of Brighton: Colonel Gray Drive (Brighton's rough north edge), Sunset Drive, Westwood and Maplewood crescents, Hope, Moreau, Brittany, Berkeley, Strathmore. 1960s-80s two-storeys, split-levels and bungalows (40% two-storey by LiDAR, median 184 m2), mature trees. Palette a guess.

Bramwell and Kenwood._comment: West Royalty north, by West Royalty Elementary: Bramwell, Silverwood, Salisbury, Commonwealth, Kenwood Circle off Sherwood Road / Lower Malpeque Road. One-storey split-entries (7% two-storey by LiDAR, median 151 m2); '4 bedroom split entry home in the sought after area of West Royalty' (12 Bramwell Street listing). Era 1990s-2000s guess, palette a guess.

Sandlewood Park._comment: West Royalty's newest planned subdivision off Upton Road: Parricus Mead, Doiron, Sandlewood, Wisteria, Thorndale, Meadow Lane, round Sandlewood Park ('one of Charlottetown's sought-after planned subdivisions in West Royalty'; one house built 2005). Big bungalows and split-entries with double garages (median 191 m2), steep roofs (LiDAR flat share 9%), stone veneer on fronts, young trees. Palette from the 2005-2020 Island norm (greige, grey, white, charcoal, navy), a guess.

Avonlea streets._comment: East Royalty north of the bypass on the west side of St Peters Road: Avonlea Drive, Rilla Road, Ingleside Drive (the Anne books' names), Angus, Darrach, Parkman, Bonnie Blink, Tara Heights; Faith Bible Church on St Peters Road. 13 Avonlea Dr built 1968, 8 Avonlea Dr 1985 (listings); median 160 m2, LiDAR top 5.7 m (bungalows, split-levels, some two-storey). Palette a guess.

Hillsborough Park north._comment: Westcomb Crescent, Oakland Drive, Cambridge Drive, Glenview Lane by Andrew's Pond and the Wright's Creek trails: Westcomb houses built 1976-77 (five listings), small low bungalows (median 127 m2, LiDAR top 4.9 m). Same look as Hillsborough Park; a centre of its own because Hillsborough Park's radius stops about 1 km short.

Parkwood and Deep River._comment: Parkwood Crescent (109 and 117 built 1972, bungalows, per listings), Hunter Lane, Deep River Drive, Seapine and Tide View courts above Wright's Creek: small bungalows (median 118 m2, LiDAR top 4.7 m), the newer courts toward the water. At the edge of Hillsborough Park's radius (about 490 m of 520); its own centre keeps the courts by the river. Palette a guess.

mail.summary: Almost all of Charlottetown and all of Stratford get their mail at Canada Post community mailboxes since 26 October 2015 (about 8,400 homes, 'close to 10,000 Islanders'; CBC). The conversion was halted the same evening nationally, but Charlottetown and Stratford had already switched; the 2018 decision was that converted addresses would not get door delivery back. So no Charlottetown street should show a mail carrier at doors, and almost no street has post mailboxes at the road.
mail.door_delivery: Effectively none for houses. Exceptions: a few addresses where a box was never put into service (Gerald Street at Upper Prince kept hand delivery after its box was pulled in 2016, CBC), apartment buildings and offices (lobby boxes), businesses downtown, and the accessibility exemption (seniors could get weekly delivery). Canada Post's 2025-26 national plan ends the rest of door-to-door delivery anyway.
mail.community_mailboxes: Everywhere else: banks of two to four grey modules with a red header band, about 1.6 m tall, 0.8 m wide each, on a concrete pad set in the grass boulevard or beside the sidewalk, usually at a corner or at a subdivision's entrance, sometimes on a side lawn of a corner house (Gerald Street protest). Ellis Road's box was 'about 15 minutes' walk' from a resident's home, and people complained of no room to pull over. Rule of thumb for a generator: one bank per 40-60 houses, within about 200 m of each, at corners on the side with the wider boulevard; in older downtown streets on a corner lot's boulevard.
mail.wall_mailbox_by_door: Older houses (pre-2015) still have the black or white metal wall mailbox by the front door, now used for flyers; new houses (2016+) have none. Shares in each yard_profile.extra.wall_mailbox_by_door.
mail.post_mailbox_at_road: Rural-style post mailboxes are a rural PEI thing (Canada Post rural routes), not a city one. In the game's map only the outermost semi-rural stretches would have any: Upton Road, outer Norwood Road, Lower Malpeque Road, Brackley Point Road and St Peters Road past the last subdivisions. The generator's mailbox_post shares are therefore 0-0.05.

carts.summary: There is no blue cart on PEI. Waste Watch is two carts plus bags: a black cart (waste) and a green cart (compost), and recyclables in translucent blue bags set at the curb on their own beside the carts (paper separately); clear bags for extra garbage in November fall cleanup. IWMC kept the blue bags in 2019 rather than buy 70,000 blue bins ('we don't need cart tipper trucks'). The existing waste_carts model is green-blue-black: replace the blue cart with one or two blue bags on the ground.
carts.collection_day: The black and green carts go out on different weeks (IWMC's app reminds people to put out 'the black or green cart'), so a street on collection day shows either green carts, or black carts with blue bags beside them, rarely all three. Carts stand at the end of the driveway, lids toward the street, handles toward the house.

school_yards.typical: A Charlottetown elementary yard: a big asphalt area at the front or side used for drop-off and play (Sherwood Elementary's drop-off area was blocked off with orange-and-black barricades and a no-parking sign to use as play space, CBC photo), basketball nets on poles on the asphalt, one main play structure and swings on wood chips edged with timbers, wooden ramps from the walkways into the chip areas (Sherwood's new inclusive playground, CBC 2025), a soccer field with metal goals, sometimes an old softball backstop, chain-link along the street side, a flagpole (Canadian and Island flags), bike racks by the door, a low name sign. Buses: yellow, Lion electric ('100% Electric', CBC photo). New schools are long two-storey boxes in red brick and grey panel (Sherwood School).

church_lawns.lawn: Suburban churches sit back on a lawn beside a big parking lot. The lawn has a low name sign near the street with a small mulched bed of day lilies or low shrubs at its foot, a flagpole now and then, a bench, a few planted trees, sometimes a playground for the Sunday school or daycare (Spring Park United has a mapped playground; Trinity has a daycare playground and community garden).

playgrounds.osm: 209 playground areas make about 75 sites (areas within 45 m merged): each site is one to seven separate surfacing pads of about 70-140 m2 (median 107 m2), a structure pad, a swing pad, sometimes a toddler pad. Most sit inside a small neighbourhood park (a grassed lot of 2,000-35,000 m2 between houses, reached from one street by a short path), at a school, or in a downtown square.
playgrounds.typical: A medium play structure (the city budgets up to $24,000 each, CBC 2020): two decks with a roof, two slides, climbing panels and activity panels, posts in green or blue (Victoria Park structure being assembled: green posts and blue decks; Victoria Park waterfront: blue posts and teal parts, CBC 2016 photos). A two-bay swing set ($2,500 budget) with two belt seats and two toddler bucket seats. Pea gravel or wood chips in a rectangle edged with 6x6 timbers (Victoria Park photo). One or two park benches, a waste bin, often a picnic table, a few young trees; in bigger parks a ball diamond backstop, a soccer field or a half-court. Connaught Square shows the newer 'natural' kind (birch log stumps, wooden balance beams) that residents pushed back against, so traditional slides and swings stayed.

street_feel: Front yards in the suburbs are open: lawn to the sidewalk or ditch, a paved driveway, a foundation bed, maybe a single spruce or maple. Fences start at the back corners of the house. A front fence or hedge is an older-neighbourhood thing (Parkdale, Spring Park, Brighton, downtown).

Back yards are where everything is: a grey-weathered board fence, a shed (red with white trim, or the house's own siding colour), a pressure-treated deck, a trampoline in family streets, a ring of chairs round a fire pit, a clothesline in older ones.
On collection day a whole street has its carts out at once, all green or all black-with-blue-bags; on other days the carts are beside the garage or against the side of the house.
No mail carrier at the doors anywhere; people stop the car at the grey mailbox bank at the corner.
Cedar hedges mark old lots: tall, dense, dark, often along a side lot line or round a back yard rather than across the front.
Robin Hood Park's streets carry the joke themselves (Sherwood: Robin, Scarlet, Friar). The East Royalty streets off St Peters Road are named from the Anne books (Avonlea, Rilla, Ingleside).
Many suburban streets have no sidewalk at all (West Royalty residents, CBC); kids ride on the road and the boulevard is a ditch line.
Fire pits are allowed in the city except during bans (Charlottetown suspended burning permits and banned outdoor fires in the dry summer of 2025, CBC).
